L275.S7: The prisoners are asked for a count in two classes of armament. The conditional opening and the distinction between great guns and small arms both belong to the reported question.
L275.S8: The privateers ask whether they can reach the people in question. The question and its object survive. One modifier describing the intended approach is generalized.
L275.S9: The interrogators ask how many men keep watch. Both names for a sentry belong to the source, which gives no answer here.
L275.S10: Dampier says the Spaniards habitually keep lookouts. The ensuing question asks how those same lookouts are managed. The subject, interrogative and passive construction survive, with a more general final predicate.
L275.S11: The question proposes two alternatives concerning the lookouts. Both infinitives, the repeated object and the conjunction survive. Each action is given a broader verb.
L275.S12: The creek, river and landing are possibilities the speakers ask about. No site is identified and no answer is supplied. The comparative judgement in “best” belongs to the speakers.
L275.S13: Dampier closes the catalogue by attributing the questions to the men’s own curiosity. That comment is part of his characterization of the interrogators.
L275.S14: The privateers compare earlier reports and ask whether any prisoner could guide a company there. Failing that, they ask where and how another prisoner capable of doing so might be taken. Dampier records their questions and subsequent planning without supplying an answer.
L299.S8: Dampier gives the staff’s length, compares it to a man’s arm and identifies a harpoon fitting at its larger end. The fitting’s particular construction is generalized.
L299.S9: Dampier names the float’s wood, places it at the other end and estimates the amount of wound line. The brackets retain the joint and the connection with the line. The second bracket continues into the following sentence.
L299.S10: The sentence continues the line’s connection to the harpoon and names its position. It then turns to the line a Moskito man holds loose in his hand. The connection and the unit of the approximate measure are generalized.
L299.S11: Events unfold after the manatee is struck. The float’s reappearance is expressed as a future outcome qualified by what may happen first. Both stages belong to the description of the hunt.
L305.S1: Dampier supplies competing names for the implement and refers the reader to a marginal figure. The measurements describe the object he says is depicted.
L305.S2: The small projection has the line and forms a joint with the striking staff. Dampier then reports the release of the iron, its movement and the animal’s inability to escape. The exact joint is generalized.
L319.S6: Dampier distinguishes the quiet attack, the retreat and the Spaniards’ inability to find the attackers. One precise dimension of the weapon is generalized.
L319.S7: Dampier compares the darts with a knitting needle and with a harpoon, names the cotton, and distinguishes what breaks from what remains in the wound. The application of the cotton, an explanation of strain, and a property chosen for the stated purpose are generalized.
L343.S6: The captain gives up his original ship and escapes in the captured sloop. Keeping both vessels distinct explains what Dampier calls a reprisal and what was left to the Dutch.
L349.S2: The crew interrupt their voyage for careening. Bringing stores ashore and putting provisions under a roof of sails are part of the same account of making camp.
L361.S2: Dampier distinguishes a place to anchor from a place suited to careening. The comparison is tied to two particular anchorages and to his estimate of the protection they afforded.
L447.S3: The islander’s ammunition runs out. Dampier lists the tools he salvaged and made and attributes his skill to time among the English. Those details account for his survival.
L447.S4: Dampier describes the islander’s habitual ironwork. The final clause distinguishes grinding pieces to an edge by prolonged labour from hardening them to a good temper as occasion required. It names these operations and their results without giving a hardening procedure.
L449.S4: Three measurements distinguish the stone tool’s length, breadth and thickness. The final qualification restricts the thickness measurement to its middle.
L449.S5: The author uses a finger as a scale in describing a hafted woodworking tool. “Helve” gives a second English name for its handle, and the last clause describes how securely it sits.
L449.S6: The negative comparison extends the narrator’s attribution of ingenuity to other peoples. His historical label and his evaluation are both attributable to him.
L449.S7: The closing first person is evidence of what Dampier says he saw and admired in Patagonia. Losing that clause would erase his basis for making the comparison.
L461.S10: “Them” refers to the seals. Dampier describes the effect of a blow on a particular part of the animal. Only the anatomical noun is generalized.
L461.S11: “Might” estimates a possible cargo. The skins, the oil and the fatness of the animals explain the commercial observation that follows the hunting passage.
L469.S2: This is a comparison between the cost of fortifying two bays and Dampier’s conjecture about their defensibility. The numbers belong to his estimate for those sites.
L469.S3: The passage offers one incident as partial evidence for the preceding estimate. One of five deserted. Four held out and were eventually taken aboard by Captain Strong.
L531.S24: A scattered group sees armed men appear, calls out to one another and goes back to its boat. The stranded boat and the two distinct groups establish the next turn in the story.
L531.S25: The boat they expected to use is already burning when they reach the bay. The sentence identifies the discovery without supplying an account of who started the fire.
L531.S26: The burial place of Captain Cook becomes a geographical landmark for the men considering how to regain their ship. Their distress and uncertainty explain why they hesitate.
L531.S27: The men fear an ambush along the wooded stretch. Dampier attributes expertise to the Spaniards. The possibility expressed by “might” matters to the account.
L531.S28: The Spaniards’ invitation to the plantations is a taunt. The wording preserves its mock politeness and the Englishmen’s silence.
L531.S29: One companion notices a rock at half ebb and likens it to a castle. Its promise as a refuge is presented as his judgement and depends on their ability to reach it.
L531.S30: Their wish to reach shelter coincides with intermittent gunfire. The whistling sound and the Spaniards’ confidence give the passage its point of view.
L531.S31: The men propose testing the depth and then discover that they can cross. The proposal and its favourable outcome are separate events.
L531.S32: The narrative gives an approximate seven-hour wait for the canoe. That duration accounts for the change of tide in the next sentence.
L531.S33: The dry rock goes under as the tide returns. The extra hour is hypothetical. Dampier uses it to compare the successive dangers from people and from the sea.
L531.S34: The Spaniards expect the water to destroy the men and stay ashore. The narrator distinguishes their few handguns from the lances carried by the others.
L531.S35: Dampier moves from a claim about skill with the lance to a biting comparison with insults. His companions’ interpretation of silence closes the passage and belongs to their perspective.
L531.S43: “Looms” are the shafts of oars. Dampier compares lancewood with young ash for straightness, then explains why privateers preferred the heavier wood and carried spare rods.
L537.S3: Dampier describes the earthwork by the eastern creek, attributes the western one to a report, and gives his estimate of their defensive strength. The comparison of numbers is hypothetical.
L537.S12: The captives explain how the governor’s warning letter led him to build the island watchhouse. The month and the four watchmen belong to their account of his orders.
L537.S13: The watchmen distinguish the ship they expected from the smaller craft they actually saw. This explains their first reading of the visitors.
L537.S14: The watchmen initially mistook the occupants of the leading canoe for shipwreck survivors. Seeing more canoes changed their minds, though Dampier says they only began to suspect the truth.
L537.S15: The captives identify the rider as a regular morning visitor and estimate his journey into town. The travel time comes from their testimony.
L537.S16: Dampier’s party briefs Eaton’s men after they land. The sentence establishes who learned the news and when.
L537.S17: The men count the hours already lost and the journey still ahead. Their conclusion was to postpone the expedition because the governor might already have received word.
L547.S1: Amapalla exceeds Mangera in size, while their soils resemble each other. The comparison changes its subject halfway through the sentence.
L547.S2: Dampier places the island’s two towns and describes the steep approach to the eastern hilltop settlement. His claim about its defensibility is an inference from the terrain.
L557.S1: Davis meant to identify himself and negotiate with the congregation, with the friar’s promised help. A crewman’s shove interrupts that intention before the townspeople have finished entering.
L557.S2: The man who was pushed runs, and the others spring out “like Deer.” Dampier preserves the contrast between their alarm and Davis, left with the friar and unaware of its cause.
L591.S1: The log dates the arrival off Payta to November 2 and records the evening landing party. Dampier gives its strength as 110 men and reports their intention to take the town.
L595.S8: The carved churches and the little seaward fort are separate observations about Payta. “No great Guns” describes the fort’s armament at the time of the visit.
L595.S9: Dampier judges what the small fort could command with the arms available there. He is estimating its reach over the bay.
L595.S10: A second fort stood above the town. The closing “both” refers to the town and the lower fort, which clarifies their relative positions.
L621.S3: “As we were afterward informed” dates Dampier’s knowledge of the bark’s purpose. The crew learned only later why it had been sent.
L621.S4: Dampier looks back on the chase his crew unexpectedly declined. He connects the mistaken belief that the coast was clear with the surprise at Puna, and presents that connection as his explanation.
L629.S7: The first lookout’s headland projects from Puna into the sea. Point Arena is the anchorage visible from it, a second geographical reference.
L629.S8: The mounted watchers ride out in the morning and return at night. This sentence describes their routine and distinguishes them from the canoe-borne sentinel.
L629.S9: Flooded mangrove country lies between the two named points. Dampier also identifies a smaller headland where the inhabitants were obliged to keep an additional watch when danger was feared.
L629.S10: The second sentinel travels by canoe because the mangrove marsh has no overland approach. The mode of travel follows from the terrain.
L647.S3: The canoes have crossed before daylight. Dampier then identifies the group they were waiting for as the people of Puna.
L647.S4: Some Puna residents arrive on their customary bark-log rafts near the end of the ebb. Dampier explicitly assigns their capture to his own men.
L647.S5: Dampier says his men captured both watchmen and all the inhabitants on the following day. “Not one escaping” gives the full scope of his claim.
L647.S6: The next ebb marks a separate seizure. Its cargo was Quito cloth, and the vessel was a small bark.
L647.S9: A canoe carries word to the bark where most of the company remain. The capture of the cloth ship supplies the time reference, and the message urges the men to hurry to the town.
L647.S10: “Riding” means lying at anchor at Point Arena. The bark subsequently comes to Puna with the men and remaining canoes on the flood tide.
L647.S11: Five men remain aboard with orders tied to the following morning. Dampier records the company’s expectation that Guiaquil would already be in their hands by then.
L647.S12: The crew seizes one of three barks transporting captive Africans. The prediction about the two still coming from Guiaquil is the captured master’s statement.
L647.S13: The party cuts down the captured vessel’s mainmast and leaves her anchored. Both verbs have the same vessel as their referent.
L647.S14: Dampier offers two explanations for the slow approach. The town may have been farther away than expected, or the crowded canoes may have rowed more slowly.
L647.S15: At daybreak the company still has two leagues to travel and little flood tide left. The captains seek the local pilot’s assistance and send revised instructions to their bark.
L647.S16: The messenger arrives too late. Dampier explains that his party and the two barks carrying captive Africans passed on opposite sides of the river without detecting each other.
L647.S17: The two barks weigh anchor and go downriver toward Puna as the tide turns. They are the same vessels the privateers had just missed.
L647.S18: The crew aboard Dampier’s bark mistakes the approaching vessels for hostile ships and fires three guns. The supposed loss of Dampier’s party was the crew’s inference.
L647.S27: “C. Davis” is Captain Davis. On his return the party agrees to go toward the town, with the express condition that it will withdraw if the town has already taken alarm.
L647.S28: The departure coincides with the flood tide. “N. E.” belongs together as the compass bearing of the channel the rowers actually used.
L647.S29: A canoe catches on a submerged stump in a fast river. The other crews save it at once. Its overturning is what Dampier thinks would otherwise have happened.
L647.S36: A man who had accused others of cowardice later admits that he secretly released the guide. His subsequent cry shifts responsibility for the cut cord onto someone else.
L649.S3: Dampier counts on the labour of captive Africans, the flour at the Galápagos, and a river for repairing ships. His closing claim about resisting Spanish forces is conditional speculation.
L671.S5: Dampier offers a third explanation for the lack of settlement. His description of the coastal peoples as hostile belongs to his account of their resistance to outsiders who came to attack them.
L671.S6: The six leagues of uninhabited woodland and the absence of an overland route explain why the river figures so prominently here. Dampier attributes the danger to the inhabitants’ enmity toward the Spaniards.
L685.S2: The crew voted to attend to their ships promptly so they would be ready when the fleet passed. Both the work and their reason for hurrying belong in the account.
L685.S3: The sailors chose the Pearl Keys for their position on the contemporary Lima–Panama shipping route. Dampier’s claim that they could hardly miss the fleet records their confidence at the time.
L723.S2: Dampier credits the captured letters with encouraging the undertakings and records their return to Portobel. His hesitation over whether the warning was prophecy or conjecture qualifies his own account.
L727.S2: La Sound learned of Wright’s agreement and persuaded about 120 Frenchmen to join the unsuccessful Cheapo expedition. The remark about recognizing European nationalities is Dampier’s explanation of how the party passed.
L739.S2: The terms of the proposed trade establish what the sailors expected to receive and where they had agreed to wait. The discrepancy in the next sentence depends on those particulars.
L739.S3: The promised cargo boat proved to be a fireship, although the hail sounded familiar. Dampier reports that the agreed word was used without giving the word itself.
L739.S4: The exchange of hails, the explosion and the hurried departure establish who acted and why the crew abandoned its anchorage. These are events witnessed from the threatened ship.
L741.S1: Dampier judges the outcome at Perico against what he imagines might have happened at Tabago. His suggested reasons for the Spaniards’ choice remain explicitly conjectural.
L743.S1: Swan saw a small float and what appeared to be a man who suddenly vanished. The sighting is distinguished from Swan’s fear of treachery and the narrator’s guess about why the man dived.
L745.S1: The narrator only supposes what the swimmer intended. The material and that uncertainty are reported, while the exact attachment point on the ship remains generalized.
L745.S2: Dampier says he was aboard Sharp’s ship at Coquimbo when an earlier fire was discovered by chance. This firsthand comparison explains his suspicion about the swimmer.
L749.S4: Dampier criticizes the gun platforms and describes what the men in his boats could do to those exposed on them. The English retains “shot” and generalizes only its identifying modifier.
L787.S1: The Lobos Islands serve as a reference for a sailing course in changeable winds. Distances, latitude and bearings belong to the pilotage account and explain the use of visibility here.
L787.S3: Dampier explicitly connects the course before Cape St. Francisco with his fear of being seen by an enemy. The sentence gives the voyage’s local setting and his reason for departing from the coast.
L813.S10: The light was the Spanish admiral’s order to anchor after dark. Its meaning establishes what the observers expected when they next saw a light.
L813.S11: The witnesses say where they first saw the light and estimate that it lasted half an hour. That timed observation precedes their later mistaken identification.
L813.S12: Dampier separates what the sailors thought they saw from what they subsequently learned about the second light. Their false impression of the fleets’ relative positions is the point of the episode.
L847.S7: The hour and the millpond comparison give a precise picture of the sudden evening calm. They help explain the crew’s reliance on rowing in the next sentence.
L847.S8: The rowers found that they could not reach shore before daylight and turned back. Their concern about being seen explains the reversal.
L847.S9: Five leagues is the crew’s estimate of their distance from land at daybreak. Dampier also records their own judgment that this was far enough.
L847.S10: The sailors meant to wait for evening, but a fiercer storm arrived at three. The comparison is with the tornado they had experienced the previous day.
L847.S15: The Spanish breastwork stood beyond the mangroves on the firm riverbank. Its stated purpose explains the structure the arriving sailors saw.
L847.S16: Dampier says the Indigenous watchmen heard the oars and ran toward León to give warning. The sentence records who first raised the alarm.
L847.S17: The landing divides the party and the testimony. Four hundred and seventy marched on the town, while Dampier stayed with fifty-nine others to guard the canoes.
L851.S1: The party left the canoes at about eight. This brief departure notice sets the clock for the account of the march to León.
L851.S2: The marching order distinguishes Townly, Swan, Davis and Knight and assigns the recorded numbers to the first three captains. These identities matter when Townly arrives ahead of the others.
L851.S3: Townly’s advance party encountered roughly seventy horsemen before reaching the city. The distances and the horsemen’s refusal to stand distinguish this encounter from the later charge.
L851.S4: Townly’s eighty entered the town at about three and met a larger body of Spanish horsemen. Dampier’s alternative estimates survive for both the Spanish force and its fallen leaders.
L851.S10: The man had declined an offer to remain ashore and later refused quarter. His spoken resolve and his death explain why Dampier singles him out in the next sentence.
L851.S11: Dampier names the dead man Swan and recalls his disposition, then distinguishes him from Smith, Captain Swan’s merchant, who was taken alive and recognized in the governor’s household.
L851.S13: Smith’s figures are his answer under interrogation. Dampier credits that answer with protecting the men at the canoes, a distinction that would disappear if the figures were presented as an actual muster.
L851.S14: Dampier attributes the governor’s inaction to alarm, while the estimate of more than a thousand men is explicitly Smith’s. The two judgments have different speakers.
L853.S4: The account identifies the Spanish defensive work, its garrison and the barrier across the creek. The claim about what ten men might have done is Dampier’s estimate, distinct from what followed.
L855.S1: Dampier says the defenders left after two shots and that the obstruction occupied his party for nearly half an hour. The figures describe the outcome of this encounter.
L855.S2: The landing leads into a march of about a mile to town. Both Rio Lexo and Rea Lejo are kept as the alternative names printed by the source.
L887.S2: After the canoes overturned, one man drowned and several men lost arms or had their supplies spoiled. The account distinguishes the death from the different material losses.
L887.S3: Townly’s party regained the beach and tried to go inland, only to find creeks they could not ford. The condition of their equipment after the capsizing and the terrain explain their return.
L929.S3: The men spent a day drying out and entered Acapulco Harbour the following night. Dampier’s comparison with seeking manatees conveys how quietly they moved.
L929.S4: Dampier locates the anchored ship in relation to the castle, town and other landmarks. His estimate of roughly a hundred yards describes the scene the party actually found.
L943.S12: Dampier traces the Spaniards’ knowledge of the ship’s signal to men captured after the rout. The signal had a meaning agreed for this particular event. A direct reading preserves who disclosed it and what the sailors thought it meant.
L943.S13: Dampier was aboard when the Spaniards made the signal. He remembers waiting and seeing the scattered men in their canoes but cannot remember why the ship held back. Both the eyewitness claim and the admission of uncertainty belong in the translation.
L943.S14: Capture or sinking is a feared outcome that never occurred. The conditional, proximity to the fort and timing of the land wind explain why Dampier believed the ship would have been trapped.
L959.S3: Swan’s position offshore, the relative spacing of the other vessels and the purpose of the watch remain explicit. The indefinite article before the distance is direct. The bracket generalizes the specified unit of spacing.
L1005.S9: Swan wanted to leave, the men insisted on bringing out the provisions, and they disregarded his order about how to take the laden horses. The disagreement and the distinction between his order and what actually happened explain the next sentence.
L1005.S10: The Spanish attack overtook the men guarding the corn. Dampier says that all of that escort died. The place and the identity and fate of this particular group can be retained directly.
L1045.S6: The shipboard judgment linked the man’s conviction for theft to a sentence carried out by the whole company. The particulars express the severity of the sentence being reported and distinguish it from the acts that follow.
L1045.S7: Swan struck first and Dampier includes himself in the company that followed. The force of “with a good will” and the narrator’s own participation are both material to this eyewitness account.
L1295.S4: Dampier contrasts the absence of pitched battles with prolonged local fighting, then explains what defeat meant when little mercy was shown. The duration, repeated skirmishes and reported violence convey his account of a custom.
L1301.S6: The gifts go to the particular boy’s father, who hosts the feast and is either the sultan or another prominent person. The time of the priest’s office belongs to the order of this ceremony.
L1301.S7: The pronoun continues to refer to the priest. The sentence describes what his office entailed at this ceremony. The reading should remain a third-person historical observation and add no procedural explanation.
L1359.S1: The prisoner is the grammatical subject but the object of the punishment. His nakedness, inability to move unaided and the time of day establish his condition at the outset.
L1359.S2: Dampier distinguishes the afternoon movement of the captive from its intended result, continued sunlight on his face. The bracket generalizes the particular movement. The fierce heat, insects and condition attached to the threatened killing remain explicit.
L1359.S4: Dampier moves from the individual prisoner to what he describes as a common punishment and a variant of it. The distinction between what was usual and what happened only sometimes, and the suffering attributed to heat and insects, carries the comparison.
L1391.S1: One servant of the General had offended, and this introductory sentence says that his punishment follows. It gives no basis for identifying the offence.
L1391.S2: A relative clause describes the servant’s situation on the boat. The edition generalizes the physical arrangement and its immediate cause. The repeated submersion and the short intervals in which he could breathe are stated directly.
L1415.S13: Dampier links the men’s restlessness to Teat’s proposal and the oath against Swan. Concern about going to sea without medical assistance delayed departure. Cookworthy’s report of an injured leg is a pretext, not an injury the narrator says occurred.
L1415.S14: The surgeon intends to come with the captain the next day and sends his assistant in his place. Naming Herman Coppinger here identifies the person who boards alongside Dampier in the next passage.
L1417.S3: Coppinger and Dampier kept what they believed was the arranged meeting. Neither suspected the scheme before reaching the ship. The first-person account establishes the limits of Dampier’s knowledge.
L1417.S4: The two men discovered why medical assistance had been requested. The canoe went ashore again and others were invited aboard while Swan was kept uninformed. These details explain the narrator’s discovery and who knew what.
L1651.S6: A shared ladder and the surrounding cliffs explain how Dampier thought the settlement protected itself above and below. The source has an unreadable word for part of the layout. A direct translation can preserve the architectural description and the gap.
L1759.S3: Dampier reports a seafarers’ belief about waterspouts and says he had never heard of the practice helping. Its supposed purpose belongs to the sailors. Its effectiveness is expressly unconfirmed.
L1837.S6: The sentence identifies the lance, its material and form, and the further hardening of its point. Only the specific treatment named after “by” is generalized.
L1837.S7: Dampier saw no metal and inferred that the people probably used stone hatchets. The comparison with America and the reference to Chapter IV support that inference without converting it into something he witnessed.
L1881.S5: Read determines how much oil to keep. The seizure of cargo, release of the damaged proa and detention of its crew are different actions. Their order and objects can be rendered directly.
L1927.S6: Dampier’s claim about recovering favour is conditional on surviving the first anger and speaking with the people concerned. His description of their conduct and the possibility of reconciliation are his assessment.
L1941.S3: Hall meant to stop a particular canoe crew from accompanying the voyagers. The sentence attributes a warning shot to him during this encounter and explains why he frightened that crew.
L1941.S4: The canoe crew’s first frightened reaction was followed by a decision to reboard and follow. The change matters because Hall’s action did not settle whether they would accompany the voyagers.
L1945.S2: Wind and the risk of capsizing influenced the party’s choice of a landing place. Dampier reports the numbers on shore as alternatives and describes the danger to the canoe and its occupants conditionally.
L1947.S3: The canoe stopped after approaching the islanders. Dampier identifies himself as the man who presented the gun, and the people on shore fell flat. The reported gesture and response belong to this specific meeting.
L1947.S4: Dampier says he meant the islanders to see that his party did not intend to hurt them. Preserve the stated intention as his own explanation, together with what he says they could see.
L1947.S5: The party rowed gently in and some people on shore withdrew. The temporal clause sets these events in order and the partitive “some” limits the extent of the withdrawal.
L1947.S6: Those still standing made gestures that Dampier interpreted as hostility. He attributes their renewed fear to his own second discharge. The distinction between visible gestures and the narrator’s interpretation is important.
L1947.S7: More of the group slipped away and the narrator estimated that five or six remained. Preserve the uncertainty of the number and the fact that a remnant stayed.
L2067.S9: The French intended to burn the Dutch commander’s ship. Dampier’s belief that greater courage might have changed the result is counterfactual. The recorded outcome is that the burning vessel was towed away and caused no damage.
L2067.S10: Dampier speculates that if the French warships had approached boldly and fought with their enemies, they might have had more success. The bracket generalizes the exact maneuver. His point about danger to his own ships remains.
L2067.S11: The actual exchange produced little gain for the French and ended in a hurried departure after about four hours. The unusual state of their sails is the evidence on which Dampier bases his characterization of their retreat.
L2161.S4: Dampier recounts the landing, the climb and Monday’s arrival at the hills in the morning. The hills, fort, coast and valley are individually named. The bracket generalizes the precise relation of the hills to the fort.
L2161.S5: The Dutch surrendered soon after the English opened fire. “From thence” refers back to the preceding location, which the edition already gives in generalized terms. The surrender itself can stand directly.
L2163.S3: Dampier describes the existing coastal guns and a smaller fort inland. The positions are observations about this particular bay and explain the opinion that follows.
L2163.S4: The assertion that the bay could not be taken by force is Dampier’s own emphatic judgment about the defenses he had described. It is distinct from an account of an attempted attack.
